a: score_values

A touchdown is 6 points, the extra point kick after it 1, a two-point conversion 2, a field goal 3 and a safety 2. If the defense returns a blocked kick or a turnover on a try all the way to the other end zone, it scores 2.
game_length
An NFL game is 60 minutes of game clock: four 15-minute quarters, with halftime after the second. Because the clock stops often, a game usually takes a little over 3 hours.
downs

The offense gets four downs (plays) to gain 10 yards. Make it and you earn a new first down; fail and the ball goes to the other team. "3rd and 5" means it is the third try and 5 yards are still needed. Teams usually punt or kick a field goal on 4th down; going for it and failing is a turnover on downs.
field_size
The field is 100 yards between the goal lines, plus a 10-yard end zone at each end (120 yards in all), and 53⅓ yards (160 feet) wide.
players_on_field
Each team has 11 players on the field at a time. Twelve or more is a penalty.
overtime

Regular season (since 2025): one 10-minute period, and both teams get a possession even if the first one ends in a touchdown; after that the next score wins, and if it is still tied when time runs out, the game is a tie. Playoffs: 15-minute periods, both teams get a possession, and they keep playing until someone wins.
play_clock
After a play ends the offense has 40 seconds to snap the ball (25 after stoppages like timeouts and penalties). Running out of time is delay of game, a 5-yard penalty.
timeouts
Each team gets 3 timeouts per half; unused first-half timeouts do not carry over. In regular-season overtime each team gets 2.
two_minute
The two-minute warning is an automatic stoppage when 2:00 remain in the 2nd and 4th quarters, almost like a free timeout.
challenges

A head coach throws the red flag to challenge a call: 2 per game, plus a 3rd if both are successful, and he needs a timeout left. Scoring plays, turnovers and every play in the final two minutes of each half and overtime are reviewed by the replay officials instead.
kickoff

Since 2024 the NFL uses the dynamic kickoff: the kicker kicks from his 35, the other players line up near midfield and cannot move until the ball lands or is touched. A kick into the end zone that is not returned is a touchback to the receiving team's 35-yard line (since 2025); one that lands short of the landing zone (inside the 20) comes out to the 40. A punt touchback comes out to the 20.
pat
The extra point is snapped from the 15-yard line (about a 33-yard kick). A two-point try is snapped from the 2-yard line.
safety

A safety happens when the offense is tackled (or fumbles out, or commits certain penalties) in its own end zone. The defense gets 2 points and the ball: the team that gave up the safety kicks it away from its own 20.
fair_catch
A returner waves an arm to call a fair catch: he cannot be hit, cannot run with the ball, and his team starts where he caught it.
turnovers

A turnover gives the ball to the other team: an interception (a defender catches a pass), a lost fumble (the ball carrier drops it and the defense recovers) or a turnover on downs. A pick-six is an interception returned for a touchdown; a strip-sack is a sack where the defender knocks the ball loose.
sack
A sack is when the quarterback is tackled behind the line of scrimmage while trying to pass. It counts as a loss of yards on that down.
penalties_common

False start (offense moves before the snap): 5 yards. Offside / encroachment / neutral zone infraction (defense): 5 yards. Offensive holding: 10 yards; defensive holding: 5 yards and a first down. Defensive pass interference: ball at the spot of the foul and a first down (at the 1 if it is in the end zone); offensive pass interference: 10 yards. Roughing the passer: 15 yards and a first down. Intentional grounding: loss of down and 10 yards or the spot of the foul (a safety if it happens in the end zone).
red_zone
The red zone is inside the opponent's 20-yard line, where most touchdowns are scored. Inside the 5 is often called the goal line. BFF counts red-zone targets and carries as part of a player's usage.
positions

Offense: quarterback (throws, runs the offense), running back (runs and catches short passes), fullback (lead blocker), wide receivers (catch passes), tight end (blocks and catches), and five offensive linemen (center, two guards, two tackles). Defense: defensive linemen (rush the passer, stop the run), linebackers, cornerbacks (cover receivers) and safeties (deep coverage). Special teams: kicker, punter, long snapper and returners.
coverage

In man coverage each defender follows one receiver; in zone each covers an area. Cover 2 splits the deep field between two safeties; Cover 3 splits it into thirds. A blitz sends extra rushers (often a linebacker or defensive back). Nickel uses a fifth defensive back, dime a sixth.
plays

Play-action: fake a handoff, then pass. RPO (run-pass option): the QB reads a defender after the snap and hands off or throws. Screen: a short pass behind blockers. Draw: looks like a pass, then a delayed run. Hail Mary: a long desperation pass to the end zone. Onside kick: a short kickoff the kicking team tries to recover. Flea flicker: a handoff, a pitch back to the QB, then a deep pass.
season_length
The NFL regular season is 17 games over 18 weeks (each team has one bye week), 272 games in all. Most fantasy leagues end in week 17.
playoffs

14 teams make the playoffs, 7 per conference: the 4 division winners (seeds 1-4) and 3 wild cards (5-7). Only the No. 1 seed in each conference gets a bye. Rounds: Wild Card, Divisional, Conference Championships, then the Super Bowl. Higher seeds host until the Super Bowl, which is at a pre-chosen stadium.
teams_count

The NFL has 32 teams in two conferences (AFC and NFC), each with four divisions of four: AFC East (Bills, Dolphins, Patriots, Jets), AFC North (Ravens, Bengals, Browns, Steelers), AFC South (Texans, Colts, Jaguars, Titans), AFC West (Broncos, Chiefs, Raiders, Chargers), NFC East (Cowboys, Giants, Eagles, Commanders), NFC North (Bears, Lions, Packers, Vikings), NFC South (Falcons, Panthers, Saints, Buccaneers), NFC West (Cardinals, Rams, 49ers, Seahawks).
dates_2026

2026 season dates (NFL.com): the trade deadline is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET; Week 18 is Jan. 9-10; Wild Card Weekend Jan. 16-18; Divisional round Jan. 23-24; Conference Championships Jan. 31; Super Bowl LXI is Feb. 14, 2027 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
most_sb
The New England Patriots and Pittsburgh Steelers have the most Super Bowl wins, 6 each (through Super Bowl LX).
draft

The NFL Draft has 7 rounds. Teams that missed the playoffs pick first, worst record first; playoff teams follow in order of how far they went, and the Super Bowl champion picks last. Extra compensatory picks (rounds 3-7) go to teams that lost more free agents than they signed. Picks can be traded.
rookie_contracts

Drafted rookies sign 4-year contracts; first-round picks also carry a fifth-year option the team can pick up. The franchise tag lets a team keep a player about to become a free agent on a one-year deal at a set (high) salary.
rosters

An NFL team carries 53 players, plus a 16-player practice squad. On game day up to 48 can be active (if 8 are offensive linemen), and a team can also name an emergency third quarterback who can only play if the other two are out.
ir_rules

A player put on injured reserve must miss at least 4 games; each team can bring back up to 8 players a season with return designations. PUP (physically unable to perform) is for football injuries that carry over from before the season; NFI is for injuries or illness not from football. BFF projects 0 points while a player is on any of these lists and starts projecting him again in his expected return week.
injury_report

On the official injury report, Out means he will not play, Doubtful means unlikely, and Questionable means uncertain. Practice reports say DNP (did not practice), Limited or Full. In 2021-2025 data, Out players played 0.1% of the time, Doubtful 0.4% and Questionable 61%, which is why BFF projects Out and Doubtful players for 0.
prime_time

Thursday Night Football, Sunday Night Football and Monday Night Football are the stand-alone prime-time games each week. In fantasy, players in the Thursday game lock first, so set those lineups early.
hall_of_fame
The Pro Football Hall of Fame is in Canton, Ohio. Players become eligible five years after they retire.
records_career
Career records: passing yards Tom Brady (89,214), rushing yards Emmitt Smith (18,355), receiving yards and total touchdowns Jerry Rice (22,895 yards, 208 touchdowns).
records_season
Single-season records (through 2025): passing yards Peyton Manning 5,477 (2013), rushing yards Eric Dickerson 2,105 (1984), receiving yards Calvin Johnson 1,964 (2012).
ppr

PPR gives 1 point per catch, half PPR 0.5 and standard 0. Most leagues also give 0.1 per rushing or receiving yard, 6 per rushing or receiving touchdown, 0.04 per passing yard (1 per 25), 4 per passing touchdown and -2 per interception or fumble lost. Pick your format with the Scoring menu and BFF re-scores everything.
flex
A flex spot can hold a running back, wide receiver or tight end. Start whoever projects highest among your non-starters.
superflex
Superflex: a flex spot that can also hold a quarterback. Quarterbacks score the most, so most teams start two and they are worth far more (set SF to 1 in BFF and values adjust).
handcuff
A handcuff is the backup to a starting running back: if the starter gets hurt, the backup inherits much of his work. Handcuffs matter most for backs who get nearly all of their team's carries.
faab_waivers

On the waiver wire, dropped and unrostered players can be claimed. With rolling priority, the team that claims moves to the back of the line; with FAAB (free agent acquisition budget), each team bids from a season budget and the highest bid wins.
bye_week
A bye week is the one week each team does not play; its players score 0 that week, so have a replacement ready.
dst_kicker

D/ST scores for sacks, interceptions, fumble recoveries, defensive and return touchdowns, safeties and few points allowed. Kickers usually get 3 for a field goal (more for long ones) and 1 per extra point. Both swing a lot week to week, so most managers draft them last and stream them by matchup. BFF does not rank them.
league_types

Redraft: a fresh draft every season (what BFF values are built for). Keeper: each team keeps a few players for next season. Dynasty: you keep your whole roster year to year, so young players are worth more. Best ball: no lineup setting; your top scorers count automatically.
adp
ADP (average draft position) is where a player usually goes in drafts. BFF's draft guide uses the FantasyPros consensus as its guide to where players go.
draft_strategy

Zero RB waits on running backs and loads up on receivers early; Hero RB takes one elite back early then waits; Robust RB takes several backs early. In one-quarterback leagues, waiting on a quarterback is usually fine because many score similarly; in superflex take two early. Try strategies against AI teams in the Mock draft.
stack_stream

A stack pairs a quarterback with his own receivers, so a big passing day counts twice. Streaming means picking up a different player each week (often a QB, TE, kicker or defense) for the best matchup.
boom_bust

A player's floor is a bad-but-realistic week (BFF uses the 10th percentile) and his ceiling a great one (90th). Boom and bust are the chances of a big week or a dud. Favored? Lean on floor. Underdog? Chase ceiling.
sleeper_term
A sleeper is a player who usually ranks outside the starter tier but should score like a starter, this week or over the season. BFF's cheat sheet lists weekly sleepers.
buy_sell_term

Buy low: a player scoring well below what his usage is usually worth (bad luck tends to even out). Sell high: scoring well above his usage, usually from touchdowns or long plays that rarely repeat. That evening-out is regression to the mean.
usage_terms

A target is a pass thrown to a player, caught or not. Target share: his share of the team's targets. Snap share: share of offensive plays he is on the field. Air yards: how far past the line of scrimmage his targets travel; aDOT is their average. WOPR = 1.5 × target share + 0.7 × air-yards share. Yards per route run = receiving yards ÷ routes. Expected fantasy points (xFP): what his targets and carries usually score given depth and field position.
advanced_terms

EPA (expected points added): how much a play changed the expected points of the drive, based on down, distance and field position. CPOE: completion % above what the throws' difficulty predicts. Success rate: share of plays with positive EPA. PROE (pass rate over expected): how much more a team passes than the situation predicts; BFF uses it for team pace and play calling.
vorp_term

VORP (value over replacement player) is the points a player should score above the best player at his position likely available on waivers. It makes up 15% of BFF value; the rest is points above the best player who would not start in your league.
vulture_committee

A vulture steals short touchdowns from the main back (often a big back or the QB). A committee splits carries between backs. Garbage time is late in a lopsided game when stats pile up against soft defense. Game script: teams that lead run more; teams that trail throw more.
ir_slot

An IR slot in fantasy holds a player your league platform lists as injured (rules vary: some allow Out, some only IR) without using a bench spot. Fantasy trade deadlines are set by each league, often around week 10-12.
fantasy_playoffs
Most leagues play the fantasy playoffs in weeks 15-17, with 4 or 6 of 10-12 teams making it. BFF's schedules show each player's matchups for those weeks.
betting_terms

The spread is the favorite's expected margin: a 3-point favorite (-3) must win by more than 3 to cover. The moneyline is a bet on who wins outright. The over/under (total) is the expected combined score. -110 means you risk 110 to win 100; the extra is the vig. A team's implied total = total ÷ 2 + spread ÷ 2 for the favorite (minus for the underdog); BFF uses it in every projection. For entertainment, 21+ where legal.
parlay_term

A parlay combines bets: all legs must win, and the payout multiplies. A same-game parlay takes legs from one game. A player prop is a bet on a player's stat, like over 64.5 receiving yards or an anytime touchdown. BFF predicts the lines and picks only where its projection disagrees enough. For entertainment, 21+ where legal.
special_teams

Special teams are on the field for kicks: the kicker (field goals, extra points, kickoffs), the punter, the long snapper (snaps the ball 7-8 yards back to the holder or about 15 to the punter), the holder (often the punter) and the returners.
eligible_receivers

Only eligible receivers may catch a forward pass: the two players on each end of the line and the backs (players at least a yard behind the line). Linemen are ineligible unless they report to the referee as eligible. A quarterback who takes the snap directly from under center is ineligible, but one lined up as a back, such as in the shotgun, can catch a pass: Nick Foles caught a touchdown on the "Philly Special" in Super Bowl LII.
win_league

Start your best projected lineup every week, work the waiver wire early in the week for players whose role just grew, trade for players whose usage is better than their points (buy low) and away from the reverse, keep a backup for your most important running back, and check your players' matchups for the fantasy playoffs (weeks 15-17) before the trade deadline.
fantasy_scoring

Typical fantasy scoring: a passing touchdown is 4 points (6 in some leagues), 1 point per 25 passing yards, an interception -1 or -2 depending on the site; a rushing or receiving touchdown is 6, 1 point per 10 rushing or receiving yards, a lost fumble -2, a two-point conversion 2. Receptions add 1 point in PPR, 0.5 in half PPR and 0 in standard; that is the only difference between the three.
